# Tetrahedral representation and traversal

## Overview
This family covers methods that decompose volumetric data into tetrahedral primitives to enable object-order rendering or precise isosurface extraction [S1]. It solves the problem of rendering unstructured or irregular grids by providing a topology that guarantees planar faces and consistent ray-cell intersection logic, avoiding the "problem cells" found in hexahedral grids [S1]. Unlike [Marching Cubes](940-marching-cubes.md), which can produce ambiguous surfaces in cubic cells, tetrahedral decomposition resolves these by subdividing cubes into tetrahedra [S1]. It differs from [Ray Marching](100-ray-marching.md) by leveraging hardware rasterization or explicit geometric traversal rather than per-pixel sampling, offering efficiency for unstructured grids [G].

## Shared principles
This family builds on the shared principles of [Cell projection](26-cell-projection.md).

## Subtopics

### [Projected Tetrahedra](877-projected-tetrahedra.md)
Projected Tetrahedra (PT) is an object-order volume rendering technique that decomposes a volume into tetrahedral cells, projects them onto the 2D image plane, and rasterizes the resulting triangles using hardware acceleration. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering unstructured or irregular grids by leveraging the graphics pipeline's scan conversion and compositing capabilities, avoiding the memory bandwidth and cache inefficiencies of ray casting. Unlike [Tetrahedral Volume Rendering](820-tetrahedral-volume-rendering.md), which may use differentiable rasterization or two-pass GPU pipelines for unstructured data, standard PT generates a continuous stream of triangles in software (or via vertex shaders) that are sorted and composited. It differs from [Marching Tetrahedrons Algorithm](940-marching-tetrahedrons-algorithm.md) by rendering the volume interior (opacity/color) rather than extracting an isosurface.

### [Marching Tetrahedrons Algorithm](940-marching-tetrahedrons-algorithm.md)
The Marching Tetrahedrons Algorithm (MTA) is an iso-surface extraction method that decomposes volumetric grid cells (typically cubes) into tetrahedra to resolve topological ambiguities inherent in cube-based methods like Marching Cubes. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using a tetrahedral decomposition to ensure consistent, planar intersections within each cell, thereby avoiding the "problem cells" where rays might intersect a face twice or where topology is ambiguous.

### [Early Tetrahedron Termination](1451-early-tetrahedron-termination.md)
Early Tetrahedron Termination is a rendering optimization technique that reduces the computational load by skipping the processing of tetrahedra that are fully occluded by previously rendered, opaque geometry. It operates on the principle that if a ray has already accumulated sufficient opacity to block further contributions, subsequent tetrahedra along that ray do not need to be evaluated. This method is distinct from general opacity culling, which removes primitives with zero intrinsic opacity before rendering; Early Tetrahedron Termination removes primitives based on the accumulated opacity of the scene during the rendering phase.

### [Adaptive Delaunay Update](4923-adaptive-delaunay-update.md)
Adaptive Delaunay Update is a strategy for maintaining the topological connectivity of a tetrahedral mesh during optimization-based volume rendering, specifically when vertex positions change dynamically. It addresses the problem of keeping the mesh valid (Delaunay) without incurring the prohibitive cost of full recomputation at every iteration. It differs from static triangulation methods by incrementally updating topology based on vertex movement thresholds, balancing GPU acceleration speed with geometric accuracy.

### [Grid-based Traversal](7083-grid-based-traversal.md)
Grid-based Traversal is a method for rendering irregular volume data (tetrahedral meshes) at interactive rates by partitioning the volume into a hierarchical grid structure to quickly determine candidate tetrahedra. It sets itself apart from its siblings by avoiding explicit connectivity information between tetrahedra, instead relying on spatial hashing into a grid to manage the large number of primitives. Unlike [Projected Tetrahedra](877-projected-tetrahedra.md), which projects primitives to screen space, this method operates in object space using ray-tetrahedron intersection tests within grid cells.

### [Parallel Projected Tetrahedra with KD-Tree Partitioning](8767-parallel-projected-tetrahedra-with-kd-tree-partitioning.md)
This method enables parallel volume rendering of large unstructured tetrahedral grids by partitioning the data using a kd-tree and applying a traditional sort-last compositing algorithm. It renders unstructured grids natively without sampling into a regular grid, avoiding the oversampling/undersampling issues and parallel distribution complexities associated with grid-based sampling approaches. Unlike other parallel rendering approaches that require continuous cell transfer, this method requires no further cell transfer once distributed; only image data is communicated between processes for final composition.

### [Tetrahedral Mesh Connectivity Encoding](8957-tetrahedral-mesh-connectivity-encoding.md)
Tetrahedral Mesh Connectivity Encoding, specifically the Basic Cut-Border Machine (CBM), is a region-growing compression scheme that encodes the connectivity of a tetrahedral mesh by traversing it and generating a stream of opcodes. It solves the problem of efficiently storing and transmitting mesh topology by describing the position of new vertices relative to a growing boundary (the cut-border). It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Projected Tetrahedra](877-projected-tetrahedra.md) by focusing on lossless connectivity compression rather than direct rasterization, and from [Marching Tetrahedrons Algorithm](940-marching-tetrahedrons-algorithm.md) by preserving the explicit mesh structure rather than extracting an isosurface.

### [Delaunay Triangulation for Tetrahedral Representation](9905-delaunay-triangulation-for-tetrahedral-representation.md)
This method constructs a tetrahedral mesh from arbitrarily distributed 3D points by enforcing the Delaunay property: no point lies within the circumsphere of any tetrahedron in the mesh. It serves as an alternative to silhouette-based methods like Visual Hull Methods (VMC), which suffer from threshold sensitivity and discontinuous surfaces. Unlike its sibling [Local Convex Hull (LCH)](11862-local-convex-hull-lch.md), which uses convex hull algorithms for local surface construction, this method relies on Delaunay triangulation to generate the tetrahedral representation.

### [TetraSDF](11632-tetrasdf.md)
TetraSDF is an analytic isosurface extraction framework for neural Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) that represents the SDF as a ReLU Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) composed with a multi-resolution tetrahedral positional encoder. It solves the problem of discretization error inherent in sampling-based methods like Marching Cubes, which deviate from the true zero-level set, and the lack of high-frequency detail capture in plain ReLU MLPs with analytic marching. It sets itself apart by preserving a global Continuous Piecewise Affine (CPWA) structure via barycentric interpolation, enabling exact zero-level set extraction without grid resolution artifacts.

### [Tetrahedral Primitive Representation](12385-tetrahedral-primitive-representation.md)
Tetrahedral Primitive Representation is a family of volume rendering techniques that decompose a volumetric dataset into tetrahedral cells to serve as the fundamental geometric primitives for projection and compositing. It solves the problem of rendering unstructured or curvilinear grids by providing a topology that guarantees planar faces and consistent ray-cell intersection logic, avoiding the "problem cells" found in hexahedral grids. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by focusing on the primitive-level data structures (such as strips, fans, or specific basis vectors) and the explicit projection of these tetrahedra to screen space, rather than just the traversal algorithm or the surface extraction logic.

### Neighbor Configuration Lookup Tables
Lookup tables defining neighbor configurations for the tetrahedral grid, divided into face, edge, and vertex neighbors, used for analytic traversal [S1]. Edge definitions are $e_0 = \{v_0, v_1\}, e_1 = \{v_0, v_2\}, e_2 = \{v_0, v_3\}, e_3 = \{v_1, v_2\}, e_4 = \{v_1, v_3\}, e_5 = \{v_2, v_3\}$ [S1]. For a tetrahedron $T$ with ordered vertices $(v_0, v_1, v_2, v_3)$, the face index $f \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$ refers to the face opposite vertex $v_f$, and the edge index $e \in \{0, \dots, 5\}$ refers to specific vertex pairs [S1]. The face neighbor lookup table (Table A6) takes tetra offset $t \in \{0, \dots, 5\}$ and local face index $f \in \{0, \dots, 3\}$ as input, and outputs neighbor index $i \ge 1$, anchor displacement $\Delta_i = (\Delta_{x,i}, \Delta_{y,i}, \Delta_{z,i}) \in \mathbb{Z}^3$, and neighbor tetra offset $t_i$ [S1]. The edge neighbor lookup table (Table A7) takes edge $(t, e)$ as input and outputs neighbor index $i \ge 1$, anchor displacement $\Delta_i$, and neighbor tetra offset $t_i$ [S1].

## Background
The use of tetrahedra in volume rendering originated from the need to handle unstructured grids and resolve topological ambiguities in regular grids [S1]. The Marching Tetrahedrons algorithm was developed as an improvement over Marching Cubes to ensure planar faces [S1]. Projected Tetrahedra was introduced to leverage hardware rasterization for unstructured data . More recent developments include TetraSDF for neural implicit surfaces [S1] and LinPrim for differentiable rendering .
